mainText:
A public inquiry into the Tom Phillips case has revealed how homeschooling exemptions let him isolate his children for four years while officials failed to review them.

New Zealand.

The Education Review Office warned Education Minister Erica Stanford months ago that oversight of homeschooled children was inadequate, before the Phillips revelations broke. Newsroom reports officials never checked Phillips's homeschooling exemptions during the four years he kept his children off the grid. Waitomo's mayor says he asked the Children's Commissioner to convene the agencies involved a year before Phillips was found, calling it a missed circuit breaker. The Prime Minister has already apologised to the children and their mother.

National has confirmed it will pursue breaking up Foodstuffs, separating Pak'nSave from New World to try to drive down grocery prices. Business groups including BusinessNZ call the plan chilling, comparing it to Labour's oil and gas exploration ban, and warn of a poor signal to investors. Winston Peters has mocked National over the policy. Newsroom reports one competition expert says Pak'nSave would emerge the big winner from any split. Labour has separately promised to ban companies from charging excessive prices. Economists remain split on whether a break-up would actually lower prices at the checkout.

The government will let councils charge developers a new infrastructure levy, with councils transitioning to the system from 2029. Councils and developers have welcomed the change, saying it cannot come soon enough given growth pressure on roads and pipes.

Aotearoa Infinite Academy, a charter school that opened this year with two hundred students, has been approved to grow to two thousand by 2027. It already has six hundred enrolled and four hundred on the waitlist, making it one of the country's biggest schools.

A scathing report into Fire and Emergency New Zealand has recommended reviewing the board and truck procurement, after thirty new trucks bought in 2019 still were not in use.

Western Bay of Plenty will hold a byelection after councillor Alan Kurtovich resigned over the council's Māori wards decision. In Tauranga, the Beach Road pōhutukawa has been poisoned for a third time, with the council saying motor oil may have been sprayed on the tree's roots.

World.

Palestinians continue moving back into northern Gaza on foot after Israel opened a crossing through the military zone bisecting the enclave. Rescuers say twenty one people, including eight children, were killed when a war damaged building collapsed in Gaza City, hit by an Israeli strike last year. Ten families had reportedly been living inside.

Rwanda backed rebels remain inside Goma in eastern Congo after overrunning Congolese troops. United Nations officials estimate more than one million displaced people are now trapped inside the designated safe haven city.

Saudi Arabia says it shot down a Houthi drone south of Mecca. The Houthis deny targeting the holy city. It comes amid rising concern over Saudi oil infrastructure, with BBC analysis warning any escalation could push up energy prices worldwide.

King Charles allegedly told Princess Diana's brother, Earl Spencer, that she would be forgotten soon enough, in a phone call in the days after her death. The claim appears in Spencer's new memoir. Buckingham Palace has pushed back, saying grief can colour memory of events.

Technology.

Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei has called for AI development to slow down, citing serious risks, while Microsoft AI head Mustafa Suleyman says rival Anthropic itself could have a disastrous impact on humanity by suggesting its Claude model may be conscious. A former Anthropic researcher told the BBC staff are genuinely frightened for humanity's future. The UK government has rejected a kill switch requirement for dangerous AI, saying it cannot simply turn AI off. United States President Donald Trump has dismissed the warnings, citing competition with China. Sam Altman says the world is right to be afraid but should trust AI firms.

Sport.

League. The Warriors play Newcastle at Eden Park on Sunday in a sudden death elimination final, sold out despite the switch to the bigger venue. Dallin Watene-Zelezniak returns to the extended squad less than four weeks after breaking his right clavicle.

Rugby. The Black Ferns have made mass changes for Sunday morning's WXV Global Series test against Scotland, their first test since 2018 under this level of experimentation from coach Dave Rennie. Dual Olympic gold medallist Whitney Hansen starts. Two potential debutants are named in the twenty three.

Formula One. Max Verstappen started an exhibition go kart race at Silverstone in one hundred and first place among amateur drivers and worked through the field in fourteen laps to win, navigating multiple pile ups along the way.

Football. Leeds United's four one win over Newcastle at Elland Road, lifting them to third in the Premier League, continues to draw scrutiny over the weekend's Manchester derby VAR error, with focus on why Enzo Fernandez's offside position was never checked before Erling Haaland's winner.

Golf. Ryan Fox says he has had no time to think about anything beyond golf since his major win, as he continues to ride the attention that followed.

Basketball. The Breakers have signed Mojave King after ruling American import Josiah-Jordan James out of the opening rounds of the NBL season with injury.

Coming up. The Warriors play Newcastle at Eden Park on Sunday. The Black Ferns play Scotland in Sunday's WXV Global Series clash. NRL finals continue this week.

End of flash.
